summary: Defines methods to make it easier to deploy certificates for TLS in multi-tenant environments, where hosted domains often end up using the host's certificate. It uses secure HTTP to establish the connection between the domain and its server.

eli5.summary: Apartment residents can prove which home is theirs rather than showing only the building's ID.

questions: how to get proper certificates in multi-tenant hosting

subtitle: Prove a hosted domain's TLS identity by publishing certificate fingerprints at a well-known HTTPS address.

tldr.problem: Hosting companies often cannot get or hold certificates for each customer's domain, so hosted services present the host's certificate and users must accept an identity mismatch.
tldr.mechanism: The customer's domain publishes a JSON file over HTTPS at /.well-known/posh/{servicedesc}.json holding certificate fingerprints, or a reference to another HTTPS location that holds them. The client compares the server's certificate to those fingerprints.
tldr.outcome: A hosting provider can use one certificate for its own name while each customer domain still vouches for it. The RFC was developed for XMPP and might suit other non-HTTP protocols.

today: RFC 7711 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no replacement or update. It was written alongside RFC 7712, which uses POSH as a prooftype for XMPP.

sections.title: The Multi-Tenant Certificate Problem
sections.content:
The RFC opens with a thought experiment. A hosting company runs a service for ten thousand customer organizations. Each customer wants the service identified by its own domain name, such as bar.example.com, not the host's name, such as hosting.example.net.

That needs TLS certificates that contain the customer's name, and the RFC lists why the hosting company cannot easily get them: certification authorities will not issue them to the host, customers worry about liability if they hand over private keys, the host does not want to hold those keys, and one certificate per customer is a large administrative load.

The fallback is a certificate for the host's name. Users then see warnings and must take a leap of faith over the mismatch. DNS Security and DANE could help, but the RFC says deploying them for all customers would take several years. POSH (PKIX over Secure HTTP) is the faster alternative. It was developed for XMPP, where it serves as a Domain Name Association prooftype (see RFC 7712), and it might be usable by any non-HTTP application protocol.
sections.eli5: A big building hosts many families, but only the building has an official ID. Families want to prove which door is theirs, and POSH gives them a way to do it.

sections.title: Fetching the Verification Material
sections.content:
The server still proves its identity by presenting a PKIX certificate during the TLS handshake, and the certificate is checked by the rules of the application protocol. What POSH changes is where the POSH client gets the material to check it against. The client sends an HTTPS GET to the source domain at /.well-known/posh/{servicedesc}.json. For a hypothetical service called SPICE and the domain bar.example.com the request is for /.well-known/posh/spice.json.

POSH servers MUST use HTTPS, and the client MUST verify the HTTPS certificate of the source domain. That step bootstraps trust for everything after it.

The source domain answers in one of three ways: with a fingerprints document, with a reference document, or with HTTP 404 Not Found if it has neither.
sections.eli5: To check a door, you first go to the family's official noticeboard, which is itself locked up safely, and read what it says about their door.

sections.title: Fingerprints and Reference Documents
sections.content:
A fingerprints document is a JSON object with a fingerprints array (at least one descriptor) and an expires number of seconds after which the material should be treated as stale. Each descriptor maps the name of a hash function, such as sha-256, to a base64-encoded hash computed over the DER encoding of the X.509 certificate. A document may list several descriptors, most relevant first, for example the renewed certificate before the one soonest to expire. Matching any one is acceptable.

A reference document instead has a url member (the member name is url, not uri, for historical reasons) pointing to an HTTPS location that holds the fingerprints, plus its own expires. The target MUST NOT itself be a reference document, which prevents circular delegation. For either kind, an expires of 0 means the material or delegation is invalid.

With a reference document, the host can replace its certificate without asking each customer to update anything.
sections.eli5: The noticeboard either shows a fingerprint of the door's key, or it says, go and look at the building's own board. A fingerprint is a short code that only the right key can match.

sections.title: Verification, Ordering and Caching
sections.content:
The client compares the certificate the POSH server presents with each fingerprint descriptor until one matches, using the hash functions it supports. If none match, the client SHOULD reject the connection, though it might still accept it if another method such as DANE succeeds. The delegation counts as secure when the server's credentials match the material, however the material was obtained.

POSH steps MUST finish before any application data is exchanged for the source domain. Clients that start the connection SHOULD do the POSH retrievals first. Where DNS SRV is used, they ideally run in parallel with SRV and address lookups, similar to Happy Eyeballs.

Clients MUST NOT cache results indefinitely. When a reference was followed, the client MUST use the lower of the two expires values. Clients SHOULD NOT rely on HTTP caching, and the web servers SHOULD send a Cache-Control header with a very short duration such as max-age=60, or no-cache.
sections.eli5: You check the noticeboard before you hand over anything private, and you do not trust an old copy forever. Check again after the date it gives.

sections.title: Guidance for Operators and Protocol Authors
sections.content:
An operator can obtain a certificate only for its own hosting service name and does not need certificates for each hosted domain. It must, however, coordinate with customers so that the right POSH document is served at each customer's domain. Errors there lead to authentication problems and certificate warnings.

Protocols that use POSH are expected to register a service name in the new POSH Service Names registry. For protocols that use DNS SRV the name SHOULD match the SRV service name. XMPP server-to-server connections, for example, use xmpp-server, giving /.well-known/posh/xmpp-server.json.
sections.eli5: The building manager has to ask each family to put up the right note, and each kind of service gets its own labelled slot on the board.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered the URI suffix posh in the Well-Known URIs registry, with the IETF as change controller. IANA also created the POSH Service Names registry. Its policy is Expert Review or IETF Review, chosen over First Come First Served so that POSH services stay consistent with this specification. Designated Experts approve or deny a request within 14 days, and requests undetermined for more than 21 days can be taken to the IESG.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of service names so nobody picks the same label twice.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
POSH adds to, and does not replace, the security rules of the application protocol. The HTTPS fetches depend on checking the web server's identity and on modern TLS practice. HSTS and key pinning can add further protection.

POSH only delivers a public key to the client. It does not let a hosted domain pass private keys to a host, and it does not do certificate enrollment with a CA.

Redirects must go to HTTPS URIs. Source domains SHOULD use only temporary redirects (302 or 307), and clients MAY treat any redirect as temporary. Clients are RECOMMENDED to follow no more than 10 redirects. Because POSH material is short-lived, operators are advised to swap out POSH documents if the hash functions are found to be subject to practical attacks.
sections.eli5: The noticeboard must be safe from tampering, and it only shows which door is yours. It never hands over your secret key.
